Escaping Plato’s Cave: JAM for Aligning Independently Trained Vision and Language Models

Lauren Hyoseo Yoon ††thanks: Use footnote for providing further information about author (webpage, alternative address)—not for acknowledging funding agencies. Affiliation: Computation and Neural Systems Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91108 Email: laurenhyoon@caltech.edu    Yisong Yue Affiliation: Computation and Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Affiliation: Pasadena, CA 91108 Email: yyue@caltech.edu    Been Kim Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: beenkim@google.com
Abstract

Independently trained vision and language models inhabit disjoint representational spaces, shaped by their respective modalities, objectives, and architectures. Yet an emerging hypothesis — the Platonic Representation Hypothesis — suggests that such models may nonetheless converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. This compatibility, if it exists, raises a fundamental question: can we move beyond post-hoc statistical detection of alignment and explicitly optimize for it between such disjoint representations? We cast this Platonic alignment problem as a multi-objective optimization task: preserve each modality’s native structure while aligning for mutual coherence. We introduce the Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM) framework that jointly trains modality-specific autoencoders on the latent representations of pre-trained single modality models, encouraging alignment through both reconstruction and cross-modal objectives. By analogy, this framework serves as a method to escape Plato’s Cave, enabling the emergence of shared structure from disjoint inputs. We evaluate this framework across three critical design axes: (i) the alignment objective — comparing contrastive loss (Con), its hard-negative variant (NegCon), and our Spread loss; (ii) the layer depth at which alignment is most effective; and (iii) the impact of foundation model scale on representational convergence. Our findings show that our lightweight Pareto-efficient framework reliably induces alignment, even across frozen, independently trained representations, offering both theoretical insight and practical pathways for transforming generalist unimodal foundations into specialist multimodal models.

1 Introduction

Neural networks trained on different modalities, datasets, and objectives typically inhabit disjoint representational spaces. Yet an emerging hypothesis suggests that these models — despite having no shared supervision, architecture, or training regime — may still converge toward a common statistical model of reality. This hypothesis is known as the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [1], whose naming is inspired by Plato’s Allegory of the Cave [2], which describes individuals who observe only shadows of objects cast on the wall of a cave and mistake these projections for the entirety of reality. In our context, training data and unimodal representations are the “shadows” or “projections” of reality. The true structure, or Platonic representation, lies behind the wall: a latent alignment of semantics that multiple models might uncover despite training in isolation.

This hypothesis has been discussed under several philosophical and empirical lenses, including convergent realism in the philosophy of science and the Anna Karenina scenario [3] in representation learning, which suggests that all well-performing models may ultimately resemble each other. However, most evidence to date remains observational, relying on statistical metrics that infer compatibility. These methods quantify correlations but do not suggest practical recipies for creating multimodal models from aligning unimodal ones. In this work, we develop a method to escape Plato’s Cave, enabling two independently trained models with different modalities to work together.

1.1 Escaping Plato’s Cave (Platonic Alignment)

Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis [1], we ask the question: “can unimodal models, trained independently on distinct modalities and objectives, nonetheless encode structurally compatible representations that can be discovered and aligned for post hoc?” We frame this goal as Platonic Alignment. To investigate this question, we develop the Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM) — a lightweight modality-specific modules that aligns frozen unimodally trained language and vision models via coordinated reconstruction and alignment objectives. Treating unimodal embeddings as fixed inputs, JAM jointly trains two modality-specific autoencoders that retain each modality’s native structure while encouraging representational coherence in their shared bottleneck. In doing so, the reconstruction objective anchors modality-specific information, while the alignment objective facilitates the emergence of shared conceptual space — a computational escape from Plato’s Cave. Our work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We introduce and compare multimodal alignment objectives – classic contrastive learning (Con), its hard-negative variant (NegCon), and our proposed Spread loss, which encourages structured alignment by leveraging the notion of shared context across texts corresponding to image. Notably, Spread loss consistently outperforms the other objectives, demonstrating the benefit of leveraging contextual structure for fine-grained alignment.

  • •

    We utilized curriculum-based approach as a probing strategy to examine how layer depth (early, mid, late) of pretrained encoders impacts alignment behavior and supervision needs.

  • •

    We analyze the role of model scale by comparing alignment performance across language backbones of varying parameter counts, revealing how scale interacts with limited supervision.

1.2 Related Work

Our work is related to two research threads: analyzing correlations between unimodal representations, and aligning different data modalities to construct multimodal models.

Testing for Alignment. Prior work in this direction has been largely diagnostic focusing on evaluating alignment between frozen features: measures such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) [4], variants of CCA (SVCCA [5], projection-weighted CCA [6]), and nearest-neighbor metrics [7, 1]. Other approaches explore probing tasks or zero-shot transfer to assess latent compatibility across modalities [8, 9]. More recently, model-stitching frameworks have examined whether independently trained sub-networks can be functionally composed to perform new tasks [3], hinting at deeper interoperability between pretrained systems but focusing on vision domain.

While informative, these methods are designed to be passive—they measure alignment but do not offer mechanisms to optimize or induce it. As a result, they may conflate superficial correlation with functional compatibility: two embedding spaces may appear statistically aligned yet remain ineffective for fine-grained multimodal tasks. Moreover, although recent state-of-the-art multimodal models (e.g., Gemini [10], GPT-4V [11], LLaMA 3 [12]) demonstrate strong cross-modal performance, they do not explicitly address the alignment dynamics between independently trained unimodal components. In contrast, our work provides a systematic and controlled framework for probing and optimizing cross-modal alignment—offering a potential design lens for future multimodal systems that build on or unify strong unimodal foundations.

Optimizing Alignment of Representations. A common framing of alignment in multimodal learning refers to the emergence of structurally coherent or comparable latent spaces across modalities, such that semantically related inputs (e.g., images and their captions) map to nearby embeddings. This framing underlies much of the recent progress in large-scale multimodal models such as CLIP [13], ALIGN [14], and BLIP/BLIP-2 [15, 16], DeepSeek [17], which are trained end-to-end using massive paired corpora using explicitly multimodal objectives. Notably, BLIP/BLIP-2 adopt a modular architecture that connects frozen vision encoders and large language models, offering design flexibility. However, the pretrained vision encoders utilized in this method is CLIP, thus inheriting CLIP’s multimodal alignment objective from the outset. In contrast, our approach begins with truly unimodal foundations—vision and language models trained independently—and investigates whether alignment can emerge post hoc, without relying on pre-imposed multimodal inductive biases.

2 Statistical Tests for Representation Alignment

Before introducing our Platonic alignment framework, we first assess the extent to which alignment between unimodal vision and language models can be detected through statistical metrics alone. We construct 3 settings differing in their underlying semantic alignment:

  • •

    Matching pairs (true positive), where the image and text both refer to the same real-world content — they form a true positive pair sharing an instance of reality (e.g., an image of a man sitting in a cave and the caption “a man sitting in a cave”). Consistent with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, these pairs should yield high alignment scores, reflecting shared conceptual grounding.

  • •

    Easy non-matching pairs (easy negatives), where the image and text are drawn from unrelated and incoherent sources — such as a white noise image paired with real text, or a real image paired with syntactically valid but semantically meaningless — representing negative pairs with no shared underlying content. These pairs should yield very low alignment scores, as they lack any shared semantic or structural foundation.

  • •

    Hard non-matching pairs (hard negatives), where the image remains fixed but the text is a hard-negative caption: a semantically similar alternative that diverges from the true caption in fine-grained details (e.g., an image of a man sitting in a cave, but the corresponding caption is "a man sitting on the moon"), thus contextually aligned but not referentially accurate. While more challenging, the PRH would still predict lower alignment scores here if the models encode referential distinctions; high scores in this case would suggest limitations of statistical metrics in capturing fine-grained semantic mismatch.

We use the 4 representation alignment metrics or scores to compare embedding spaces: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) [18], Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [4], SVCCA [5], and CKNNA [1]. (Metrics formulation in Appendix.)

2.1 Data & Model Set-up

We use the SugarCrepe benchmark [19] — a dataset designed to test fine-grained vision-language compositionality. Given an image, the task requires selecting between the correct positive caption and a hard negative caption. These negative captions are carefully constructed to differ from the correct caption through minimal, often localized compositional changes. This setup is ideal for evaluating models that aim to resolve fine-grained semantic distinctions rather than broad categorical matches.

SugarCrepe [19] defines seven types of hard negative captions, categorized under three compositional transformation families:

  • •

    Replace (R): Substitutes an atomic concept—attribute, object, or relation—with an incorrect alternative (e.g., “a white cave” → “a brown cave”). Includes Replace-Att (RA), Replace-Obj (RO), and Replace-Rel (RR).

  • •

    Swap (S): Exchanges two elements of the same type, altering structure while preserving content (e.g., “a man in the cave” → “the cave in a man”). Includes Swap-Att (SA) and Swap-Obj (SO).

  • •

    Add (A): Inserts a new, incorrect concept into the caption, introducing subtle mismatches (e.g., “a man on the moon” → “a man on the blood moon”). Includes Add-Att (AA) and Add-Obj (AO).

With this data, we extracted text embeddings (of all hidden states/layers) and image embeddings (CLS token embeddings of all hidden states/layers) from unimodally pretrained language and vision models, respectively. Pretrained unimodal models utilized for all the experiments are: Gemma2 (2B) [20], Llama3.2 (1B) [12], OLMo2 (7B) [21] for language models, and DINOv2 (ViT-B) [22] for vision model. With the extracted feature representations, let DD be the whole data, and BB be the batch. We construct DD in the nested pair format: D={(vi,(lPi,lNi)}i=1nD=\{(v_{i},(l_{P_{i}},l_{N_{i}})\}_{i=1}^{n} (Refer to Table 5 for variable descriptions). C⁡(i)C(i), the set of similar context text embedding for anchor ii, is defined as lPil_{P_{i}} and its hard negative lNil_{N_{i}} (i.e., C⁡(i)={lPi,lNi}C(i)=\{l_{P_{i}},l_{N_{i}}\}). Accordingly, C~​(i)=L∖C​(i)\widetilde{C}(i)=L\setminus C(i).

2.2 Results: Statistical tests detect alignment, but not in a fine-grained manner.

The results (Fig.1) show that all models reliably distinguish between matching pairs and easy non-matches, with statistical metrics consistently reflecting lower similarity scores for mismatched pairs. This indicates that even when trained independently, vision and language models encode representations that reflect a shared high-level structure. This observation aligns with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis[1], which suggests that different modalities—despite being trained with distinct objectives—can converge toward a common statistical model of reality, enabling coarse-grained compatibility across unimodal representations.

However, we observe a compelling pattern in the hard non-match condition: statistical similarity metrics yield scores nearly indistinguishable from the scores of true matching pairs. Rather than indicating a failure of alignment, this observation reveals an important insight into the statistical tests and its interaction with the hard negatives: hard negative examples’ semantic content overlaps extensively with the positive pairs at the global contextual level, differing only in fine-grained attributes. Thus, we conjecture that the representational similarity is real and consistent with shared underlying structure, but it may not be fine-grained enough to capture discriminative semantic detail. This exposes a key limitation of statistical metrics: while they can reveal high-level compatibility, they obscure nuanced yet critical distinctions for fine-grained alignment. To move beyond this limitation, we turn to a lightweight post-hoc training approach that explicitly optimizes for semantic coherence, both globally and locally. This insight directly led to our alignment training scheme in the next section.

3 Our method: Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM)

Our approach learns a joint autoencoder across two disjoint pre-trained models, as shown in Figure 2. We first utilize a modality-specific autoencoder for each pre-trained model which distills di​n​p​u​t→dl​a​t​e​n​td_{input}\rightarrow d_{latent}, which can be viewed as a form of statistical regularisation reminiscent of PCA [23, 24]: the network is encouraged to find a compact set that preserve essential variance while discarding noise through reconstruction loss (i.e., MSE Loss). The joint training objective then contrastively pulls the latent vectors from matched image–text pairs together and push hard-negatives apart. Thus, the respective autoencoders have two objectives: denoising for each modality as well as optimizing for cross-modal relation (the exact loss functions below).

The encoder follows a “funnel” layout: a sequence of fully connected layers that progressively reduce the dimensionality of the input embedding, each stage wrapped in LayerNorm for stable statistics [25], a SwiGLU non-linearity for gated expressiveness [26], and dropout for regularisation. After every dense layer, a lightweight MLP residual block [27] re-injects the intermediate representation back into itself, ensuring gradient flow. Passing through these hidden layers, in a bottleneck stage, a final linear projection maps the hidden width to the fixed latent size. The decoder mirrors the encoder, walking back through the hidden sizes in reverse. Together, we chose this design to be an effective framework for building compact yet powerful module that fits both high-dimensional text and vision representations (i.e., embeddings). In our experiments, we used 3 hidden layers with dimension size of 512, and bottleneck dimension size as 256.

3.1 Loss functions

We develop a few ideas for loss function, some of which are leveraging existing work and others developed for JAM. We introduce Contrastive and Negative Contrastive loss which are used as a baseline as well as inspire our final loss: Spread Loss functions for vision-to-language and language-to-vision. Having a set of losses designed to optimize different aspects of the alignment had a side benefit of helping us to diagnose and analyze experiments (e.g., which layer to establish alignment), as will be shown in later sections.

Contrastive Loss (Con)

Same as the contrastive loss for training CLIP model [13], we formulate our contrastive loss (ℒc​o​n\mathcal{L}_{con}), in a symmetric fashion, designed to enforce bidirectional consistency between images and texts: Vision-to-Language (VL) as matching each image with its corresponding text, and Language-to-Vision (LV) as matching each text with its corresponding image. We then leverage cross-entropy to maximize the similarity between the correct pairs while minimizing the similarity between incorrect pairs. The cross-entropy loss is given by ℒ=−∑i=1Nyilogpi\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}y_{i}\log p_{i}, where yiy_{i} is the ground truth label (yi=1y_{i}=1 for the correct pair and yi=0y_{i}=0 for incorrect pairs), pip_{i} is the predicted probability of the correct pair. Thus, the final contrastive loss is formulated as: ℒc​o​n=12​[ℒVL+ℒLV]\mathcal{L}_{con}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VL}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}\right]. where image-to-text loss (VL) and text-to-image (LV) loss are the following, respectively:

ℒVL=−1N∑i=1Nlogσ⁡(vi,lPi)∑j=1,j≠iNσ⁡(vi,lPj),ℒLV=−1N∑i=1Nlogσ⁡(lPi,vi)∑j=1,j≠iNσ⁡(lPi,vj)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{VL}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\sigma(v_{i},l_{P_{i}})}{\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{N}\sigma(v_{i},l_{P_{j}})},\hskip 8.50012pt\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\sigma(l_{P_{i}},v_{i})}{\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{N}\sigma(l_{P_{i}},v_{j})}\end{split} (1)

Here, we denote σ⁡(x,x′)=exp⁡(sim​(x,x′)/τ)\mathcal{\sigma}(x,x^{\prime})=\exp(\text{sim}(x,x^{\prime})/\tau), where x,x′x,x^{\prime} are the modality-specific embeddings (in this case, text and image embeddings, respectively), and τ\tau is the temperature parameter that controls the sharpness of the similarity distribution. For all the experiments, we set τ=0.07\tau=0.07, as done in  [13].

Negative Contrastive Loss (NegCon)

The standard CLIP objective treats all non-matching text descriptions as implicitly negative, but without distinguishing between truly unrelated captions and hard-to-distinguish negative examples (hard negatives)—those that share high semantic similarity with the positive caption but are incorrect due to fine-grained distinctions (e.g., a location or object mismatch). This lack of granularity can lead the model to underutilize structurally informative negative samples. We address this challenge by introducing NegCon loss (LN​e​g​C​o​nL_{NegCon}), which allows hard negative texts to also be penalized in the image-to-text direction, while keeping the text-to-image direction unchanged for stability. This loss scheme to incorporate hard negative texts is what has been used in the development of NegCLIP [28].

For the vision-to-language direction, we extend the candidate pool of possible text matches by concatenating both positive and hard negative captions, effectively doubling the number of candidates: The image-to-text loss is then defined as:

ℒVL=−12​N∑i=1Nlogσ⁡(vi,lPi)∑j=1,j≠i2​Nσ⁡(vi,lj)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{VL}}&=-\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\sigma(v_{i},l_{P_{i}})}{\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{2N}\sigma(v_{i},l_{j})}\end{split} (2)

This formulation explicitly anchors the image to its positive caption while contrasting it against a broader and more semantically informative set that includes hard negatives.

For the language-to-vision direction, we retain a standard CLIP-style formulation, utilizing ℒLV\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}} utilized in ℒc​o​n\mathcal{L}_{con}. Since hard negative captions have no associated image, we only use positive captions and match them against the corresponding images.

The final NegCon loss is: ℒN​e​g​C​o​n=12​[ℒVL+ℒLV]\mathcal{L}_{NegCon}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VL}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}\right]. This symmetric structure ensures that both modalities contribute to alignment, while the asymmetry in negative usage avoids destabilizing supervision on text inputs with unknown image counterparts. Hence NegCon provides a minimally modified but effective baseline for studying the role of hard negative supervision.

Spread Loss

Recall that our objective is to develop a loss function that more faithfully captures the structure of semantic similarity and fine-grained contrast in multimodal representation learning. Specifically, we aim to align image and text embeddings in a way that accounts for both shared contextual meaning and localized distinctions (fine-grain). Standard contrastive losses treat all non-matching text as equally negative, which neglects the semantic proximity of hard negatives—text descriptions that differ from the correct caption only in fine detail.

To address this, we introduce ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread}, a contrastive objective that incorporates a notion of context similarity and fine-grained differentiation. The core idea is to pull together all semantically similar captions, including the ground-truth caption and selected hard negatives, and then selectively push apart fine-grained distinctions within that similar group. This two-stage formulation allows us to preserve shared contextual alignment while enforcing discriminative power at the instance level. The idea of spread loss has been proposed in the domain of visual representation learning [29, 30], which is a variant of Supervised Contrastive (SupCon) loss [31], but tailored to tackling class collapse. We take inspiration from that work and apply this idea to the multi-modal alignment problem.11 1 We provide a parallel comparison between ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} of multimodal representation space (i.e., ours) and ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} of visual representation domain [29, 30] in the Appendix. Our ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} is formulated as: ℒs​p​r​e​a​d=12​[ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL+ℒLV]\mathcal{L}_{spread}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}\right] where ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL=(1−α)​ℒC​o​n​C​o​n+α​ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}=(1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} and ℒLV\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}} is from (1).

Spread Loss – Vision-to-Language (VL): ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}
ℒC​o​n​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{ConCon} : ConCon (i.e., Context Contrastive) lumps the positive & hard negative (which share contextual attributes) case as the similar context set and tries to push this set away from all other text embeddings. The objective of this loss is to introduce the global learning scheme where we focus on learning what is easily differentiable. Formally, we construct the loss as follows:

ℒC​o​n​C​o​n​(i,B)=−1|CL​(i)|∑cl∈CL​(i)logσ⁡(vi,cl)σ⁡(vi,cl)+∑cl~∈CL~​(i)σ⁡(vi,cl~)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}(i,B)&=-\frac{1}{|C_{L}(i)|}\sum_{c_{l}\in C_{L}(i)}\log\frac{\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})}{\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})+\sum_{\widetilde{c_{l}}\in\widetilde{C_{L}}(i)}\sigma(v_{i},\widetilde{c_{l}})}\end{split}

ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} : We introduce this second term for local learning scheme. We perform an InfoNCE-style objective, explicitly highlighting the true positive as the only “correct” text. The negative text embedding, though labeled as ’similar context’, is still in the denominator and is therefore treated as incorrect text.

ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E​(i,B)=−log⁡σ⁡(vi,lPi)∑cl∈CL​(i)σ⁡(vi,cl)\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE}(i,B)&=-\log\frac{\sigma(v_{i},l_{P_{i}})}{\sum_{c_{l}\in C_{L}(i)}\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})}\end{split}

The final formulation for VL direction is a weighted sum: ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL=(1−α)​ℒC​o​n​C​o​n+α​ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}=(1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE}, where α\alpha controls the trade-off between context-level alignment and intra-context contrast. While ℒC​o​n​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{ConCon} allows similar context to be close, ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} prevents representation collapse in similar context embeddings. Thus, ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} enables learning representations that are not only globally aligned across modalities but also sensitive to subtle mismatches in local content. In our experiments, we use α=0.5\alpha=0.5 to balance the two VL components.

Spread Loss – Language-to-Vision (LV): ℒLV\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}
Since we aim to preserve bidirectional learning throughout the joint-AE training, for the LV direction, we align positive text to its corresponding image and penalize non-matching texts (excluding hard-negative texts since there are no matching images) using a standard contrastive approach. Hence, it stays the same as ℒLV\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}} used in ℒC​o​n\mathcal{L}_{Con} and ℒN​e​g​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{NegCon}.

4 Experiments

We adopt the same data set-up as in the statistical tests, splitting each dataset into 70-15-15 train/validation/test splits. For each task, we train our Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM) with Spread loss for 100 epochs with a batch size of 32, using data seeds 5, 42, and 55. Both autoencoders are optimized jointly using AdamW [35] with gradient clipping (1.0) and a cosine annealing scheduler. The reconstruction loss is weighted by a linearly decaying factor λ⁡(t)\lambda(t), decreasing from 1.0 to 0.1 over training epochs to gradually emphasize the alignment objective. Every five epochs, we compute image-to-text Recall@1 on the validation set, applying early stopping if no improvement is observed for five consecutive validations. We evaluate on two retrieval settings: (1) binary choice between the positive and its hard negative (standard in fine-grained evaluation [19, 28]), and (2) a 5-way choice including three additional distractors. All reported results are averaged across the three seed runs.

To contextualize our approach—designed to escape the “Platonic cave” of unimodal models through post-hoc alignment—we also compare against CLIP [13], a model natively trained for multimodal representation learning. For fairness, we fine-tune CLIP on the same train/val/test splits.

4.1 Does JAM enable escaping Plato’s Cave?

Our experiment results (Table 2) show that the proposed Spread loss consistently outperforms both the Con and NegCon baseline across retrieval and alignment tasks. This improvement can be attributed to the explicit supervision embedded in Spread, which leverages the notion of “similar context”—a structured grouping based on the similarity of data points. While Con and NegCon optimize for alignment using only pairwise correspondence (and in NegCon’s case, further incorporating explicit hard-negatives), they lack a mechanism for more fine-grained context understanding. Spread, in contrast, directly encourages modality-specific embeddings to reflect not only pairwise similarity, but also semantic proximity across local clusters, resulting in better fine-grained alignment.

Despite its simplicity, our Spread-trained JAM achieves competitive performance not only compared to other contrastive loss variants, but also relative to strong baselines including pretrained and fine-tuned CLIP models. While CLIP benefits from large-scale multimodal training using massive paired datasets and purpose-built architectures, our approach takes an economical path. We do not rely on large-scale image–text corpora or models explicitly designed for multimodal integration. Instead, we build on pretrained unimodal foundations, aligning them post hoc via a lightweight, task-specific joint autoencoding strategy; much cheaper than training both from scratch. This specialist alignment approach sidesteps the need for end-to-end multimodal retraining and architectural entanglement, offering a more economical and modular alternative to generalist training. Our results suggest that meaningful cross-modal structure can emerge through structured alignment—without requiring scale, paired data, or multimodal pretraining.

4.2 What kind of supervision is useful for different layer depth?: Layer-Wise Probing via Curriculum Learning

The previous formulation (Table 2) uses a fixed α=0.5\alpha=0.5, allowing our jointly trained text and image autoencoders to equally benefit from both components of the ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} — the context-based alignment across modalities and the fine-grained contrastive supervision within semantically similar groups. While this balanced configuration offers strong performance across tasks, it treats the trade-off between coarse and fine supervision as static. However, the optimal degree of contextual separation may not be uniform across all settings — in particular, it may vary depending on the stage of representation (i.e., intermediate layers of pretrained backbones) used from each modality.

To investigate this, we move beyond a fixed-α\alpha formulation and adopt curriculum learning [36] as a probing framework (Fig. 5, 5). Curriculum learning [36] is a training paradigm inspired by human learning, where models are first exposed to easier concepts or objectives and gradually introduced to harder or more nuanced distinctions. The motivation is to guide optimization along a smoother path: by focusing early training on easier, more generalizable patterns, the model establishes a robust representational foundation before facing fine-grained or ambiguous cases. We use curriculum learning as a diagnostic framework to probe the nature of supervision required for aligning multimodal embeddings. Specifically, we vary the balancing parameter α\alpha in ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread} to control the emphasis between broad semantic alignment (ConCon) and fine-grained contrast (ContextNCE).

On the inverse relationship between α\alpha and separability

By applying this curriculum across embeddings extracted from early, mid, and late layers of both vision and language models, we observe that earlier layers consistently require higher α\alpha to achieve optimal alignment — i.e., the epoch where the model achieves the best retrieval accuracy (Fig. 5, 5). This trend aligns with the findings from concept interpretability studies (e.g., TCAV [37], Network Dissection [38]), which show that lower layers tend to represent primitive or entangled features, requiring stronger supervision to isolate meaningful concepts. In our case, increasing α\alpha acts analogously — providing finer discriminative signals that help disentangle and align early-layer representations across modalities. In contrast, later-layer embeddings — which are already more abstract and task-aligned — can be aligned effectively with less need for explicit intra-context separation. Notably, we also observe that retrieval performance improves progressively from early to late layers across all task types and model pairings. This suggests that deeper layers not only require less contrastive supervision but also encode more directly alignable representations. Thus, our use of curriculum serves as a controlled lens into the nature of supervision required at different levels of abstraction, offering insight into how independently trained vision and language models organize information across depth.

4.3 Does JAM performance scale with backbone models’ scale?

To investigate whether increasing the scale of pretrained language backbones improves alignment in our JAM framework, we conduct experiments using three models of varying size: For language models, Gemma2 (9B), LLaMA 3.2 (3B), and OLMo2 (13B), and for vision model, DINOv2 ViT-L. The objective is to understand how representational capacity – where models are trained with larger parameters and embedding dimensions– affects fine-grained multimodal alignment when trained using different contrastive optimization objectives. Gleaned from the results in Table 3, we observe that increasing model scale does not consistently lead to improved performance, regardless of the contrastive method used. The performance of Spread loss remains robust and consistently strong, but the gains from moving to larger-scale language models are minimal or negligible.

One potential reason for this plateau in benefit lies in the data regime. The training set for these spatial reasoning tasks is relatively small, typically in the range of 200 to 1000 image–text pairs. Large pretrained models are known to require substantial fine-tuning data to fully leverage their representational capacity. In our case, the limited data may not provide enough gradient signal for the larger models to differentiate themselves, effectively neutralizing their potential advantage. Another explanation relates to the nature of the task itself. These spatial reasoning benchmarks are fine-grained and often involve small semantic distinctions (e.g., between spatial prepositions or swapped object attributes). Such tasks demand precise local alignment rather than broad generalist knowledge. As a result, the inductive strengths of larger models trained on general web-scale corpora may not translate to meaningful improvements. This reinforces the utility of our task-specific Spread loss, which is explicitly designed to handle such nuanced contrasts.

5 Conclusion / Future Directions

Through this framework, we provide empirical evidence and insight into the nature of representational convergence. We show that, despite originating from disjoint modalities and being trained independently, unimodal representations can be aligned through post hoc joint autoencoding — revealing a Platonic representation that supports cross-modal coherence. We propose a practical model training recipe: the Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM), a Pareto-efficient framework for building specialist multimodal models on top of frozen unimodal foundations. Our findings show that post-hoc alignment via lightweight adaptation and structured supervision (i.e., ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread}) can rival or even outperform generalist architectures in specialist settings. Looking forward, we see JAM as a flexible testing ground for modality alignment under varying supervision regimes.

There are many directions for future work, including extending to domains that demand either highly specific reasoning (e.g., legal, medical, scientific), scaling to larger datasets and models, as well as exploring more sophisticated alignment approaches beyond our Spread loss. At larger scales, it becomes interesting to also compare accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs versus other approaches such as adapter-based and joint-training approaches. Additionally, studying these questions for more than two modalities simultaneously can be interesting, such as for time series [39, 40, 41, 42].

Contents

Appendix A Impact Statement

Platonic Alignment: Escaping the Plato’s Cave.

Platonic Representation Hypothesis [1] suggests that vision and language models, though trained on disjoint objectives and data, encode latent geometries that are mutually compatible. Our work turns this philosophical and observational claim into practice: we escape Plato’s Cave by surfacing shared structure from representations originally confined to separate unimodal worlds, while keeping every pretrained unimodal backbones completely frozen.

Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM).

We propose JAM, a post-hoc adaptor for platonic alignment that:

  • •

    Preserves specialization – Modality-specific autoencoders reconstruct each latent space, guarding task-relevant features.

  • •

    Enforces cross-modal coherence – Our novel spread loss couples the JAM framework, amplifying the latent commonality predicted by the Platonic hypothesis.

  • •

    Light-weight framework – no end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning (nor pre-training); refer to D.2 that shows the lightweight structure of JAM.

Contributions.

  • •

    Platonic Alignment through Specialist Task Settings: We test the platonic alignment through both statistical and model-training framework in specialist task settings which require more fine-grained contextual understanding of the data.

  • •

    Revisiting multimodal training pipeline strategy: Our results show that aligning the frozen pretrained backbones can rival with inherently multimodal models, charting a potential alternative strategy for creating multimodal models for specialized task frameworks.

Appendix B Statistical Metrics to Measure Platonic Alignment

B.1 Thematic analysis of statistical representation alignment tests

We focus on the following four statistical metrics for testing Platonic alignment: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA [18]) with linear and kernel (rbf kernel) PCA, Singular Value CCA (SVCCA [5]), Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA [4]), and Centered Kernel Nearest Neighbors Alignment (CKNNA [7, 1]).

The following are the thematic analyses that demonstrate our metrics selection strategy:

  • •

    Unsupervised and second-order: All four metrics are unsupervised and based on second-order statistics (e.g., inner products or covariances), making them scale-invariant and naturally comparable across modalities.

  • •

    Symmetricity: The symmetry property indicates that the metric treats the data points interchangeably, meaning OPENd⁡(x,y)=d⁡(y,x))d(x,y)=d(y,x)).

  • •

    Data-Driven (D) vs. Canonical (C):

    • –

      Data-Driven metrics (CCA, SVCCA) learn linear projections from the data that actively mold one representation space to align with another. They measure the best-case alignment achievable through adaptation.

    • –

      Canonical metrics (CKA, CKNNA) keep the input representations fixed and evaluate the existing alignment structure as is, without transformation. They quantify inherent similarity without retraining or reprojecting.

  • •

    Global (G) vs. Local (L):

    • –

      Global metrics (CCA, SVCCA, CKA) aggregate information across all sample pairs, capturing holistic alignment patterns between entire distributions.

    • –

      Local metrics (CKNNA) focus on localized structure by comparing only mutual kk-nearest neighbors, revealing fine-grained neighborhood-level similarity that may be obscured globally.

  • •

    Batchable: A computational property that makes it feasible to compute in a reasonable time frame.

B.2 Metrics Formulation

Recall our glossary:

Kernel preliminaries

Let {(𝐱i,𝐲i)}i=1n\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be paired samples: in our case, let xix_{i} be the images and yiy_{i} be the corresponding texts. A representation function fV:𝒳→V∈ℝdf_{V}:\mathcal{X}\!\to\!V\in\mathbb{R}^{d} maps inputs to feature vectors vi=fV​(𝐱i)v_{i}=f_{V}(\mathbf{x}_{i}) in an RKHS (Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space) ℋ\mathcal{H} [43] equipped with the inner-product kernel Ki​j=κ⁡(vi,vj)=⟨vi,vj⟩K_{ij}=\kappa(v_{i},v_{j})=\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle. Analogously fLf_{L} maps 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i} to lil_{i} with kernel Li​j=⟨li,lj⟩L_{ij}=\langle l_{i},l_{j}\rangle. Center both kernels to remove mean effects via the centring matrix H=I−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤H=I-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}:

K¯=H​K​H,L¯=H​L​H.\bar{K}=HKH,\qquad\bar{L}=HLH.

B.2.1 Centered-Kernel Alignment (CKA)

CKA [4] normalises the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [44] between the centred kernels:

HSIC⁡(K,L)\displaystyle\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L) =1(n−1)2​tr⁡(K¯​L¯),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(n-1)^{2}}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\bar{K}\,\bar{L}\bigr), (3)
CKA⁡(K,L)\displaystyle\operatorname{CKA}(K,L) =HSIC⁡(K,L)HSIC⁡(K,K)​HSIC⁡(L,L).\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,L)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{HSIC}(K,K)\,\operatorname{HSIC}(L,L)}}. (4)

Expanding the trace in (3) shows that every pair (i,j)(i,j) contributes a product of centered similarities:

tr⁡(K¯​L¯)=∑i=1n∑j=1n(⟨vi,vj⟩−𝔼ℓ​⟨vi,vℓ⟩)​(⟨li,lj⟩−𝔼ℓ​⟨li,lℓ⟩).\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\bar{K}\bar{L})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle-\mathbb{E}_{\ell}\langle v_{i},v_{\ell}\rangle\bigr)\bigl(\langle l_{i},l_{j}\rangle-\mathbb{E}_{\ell}\langle l_{i},l_{\ell}\rangle\bigr). (5)

Because the denominator applies the same operation to each modality, CKA is scale-invariant and bounded in [0,1][0,1]; it therefore has advantage in measuring global geometric correspondence. However, equation (4) aggregates all pairwise relations, so even a small region of mis-aligned samples suppresses the score which CKA can be too strict for measuring cross-modal cases.

B.2.2 Centered-Kernel kk-NN Alignment (CKNNA)

To focus on local structure, the authors in [7, 1] suggest a binary mask α⁡(i,j)\alpha(i,j) that selects only pairs that are mutual kk-nearest neighbours in both modalities:

α⁡(i,j)\displaystyle\alpha(i,j) =[vj∈kNN(vi)∧lj∈kNN(li)∧i≠j].\displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\!\bigl[v_{j}\!\in\!\text{kNN}(v_{i})\ \wedge\ l_{j}\!\in\!\text{kNN}(l_{i})\ \wedge\ i\neq j\bigr]. (6)

Using this mask, one can restrict the definition of alignment to bias more towards the local structure through replacing the full HSIC trace by a masked cross-covariance.:

Alignlocal⁡(K,L)\displaystyle\operatorname{Align}_{\text{local}}(K,L) =∑i=1n∑j=1nα⁡(i,j)​(⟨vi,vj⟩−𝔼ℓ​⟨vi,vℓ⟩)​(⟨li,lj⟩−𝔼ℓ​⟨li,lℓ⟩)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha(i,j)\bigl(\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle-\mathbb{E}_{\ell}\langle v_{i},v_{\ell}\rangle\bigr)\bigl(\langle l_{i},l_{j}\rangle-\mathbb{E}_{\ell}\langle l_{i},l_{\ell}\rangle\bigr) (7)
=∑i=1n∑j=1nα⁡(i,j)​K¯i​j​L¯i​j.\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha(i,j)\,\bar{K}_{ij}\,\bar{L}_{ij}. (8)

The final formulation of CKNNA becomes:

CKNNA⁡(K,L)\displaystyle\operatorname{CKNNA}(K,L) =Alignlocal⁡(K,L)Alignlocal⁡(K,K)​Alignlocal⁡(L,L).\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Align}_{\text{local}}(K,L)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Align}_{\text{local}}(K,K)\,\operatorname{Align}_{\text{local}}(L,L)}}. (9)

Note that CKNNA\operatorname{CKNNA} can be fully recovered to CKA\operatorname{CKA} for k→nk\!\to\!n, since α⁡(i,j)=1\alpha(i,j)\!=\!1 for all i≠ji\!\neq\!j.

Thus, CKA asks: “Are the two representations globally linearly related?”; whereas CKNNA captures: “Do the two models agree locally (i.e., on each point’s neighbours)?”.

B.2.3 CCA (Canonical Correlation Analysis)

Let X∈ℝdx×nX\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times n} and Y∈ℝdy×nY\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}\times n} be column-wise zero-centered feature matrices produced by two representations (all means are removed so that covariance estimates are unbiased). Define sample covariance blocks:

Σx​x=1n​X​X⊤,Σy​y=1n​Y​Y⊤,Σx​y=1n​X​Y⊤.\displaystyle\Sigma_{xx}=\tfrac{1}{n}XX^{\!\top},\quad\Sigma_{yy}=\tfrac{1}{n}YY^{\!\top},\quad\Sigma_{xy}=\tfrac{1}{n}XY^{\!\top}. (10)

CCA searches for weight vectors 𝐰∈ℝdx\mathbf{w}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, 𝐯∈ℝdy\mathbf{v}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} that maximise the Pearson correlation between projected variables:

ρ\displaystyle\!\!\rho =max𝐰,𝐯⁡𝐰⊤​Σx​y​𝐯𝐰⊤​Σx​x​𝐰​𝐯⊤​Σy​y​𝐯\displaystyle=\max_{\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}}\;\;\frac{\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\Sigma_{xy}\mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\Sigma_{xx}\mathbf{w}}\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^{\!\top}\Sigma_{yy}\mathbf{v}}} (11)
s.t.𝐰⊤​Σx​x​𝐰=1,𝐯⊤​Σy​y​𝐯=1.\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\Sigma_{xx}\mathbf{w}=1,\;\mathbf{v}^{\!\top}\Sigma_{yy}\mathbf{v}=1. (12)

Using Lagrange multipliers we obtain the generalized eigenvalue problem:

(Σx​x−1​Σx​y​Σy​y−1​Σy​x)​𝐰=ρ2​𝐰,𝐯=ρ−1​Σy​y−1​Σy​x​𝐰,\displaystyle\bigl(\Sigma_{xx}^{-1}\Sigma_{xy}\Sigma_{yy}^{-1}\Sigma_{yx}\bigr)\mathbf{w}\;=\;\rho^{2}\,\mathbf{w},\quad\mathbf{v}=\rho^{-1}\Sigma_{yy}^{-1}\Sigma_{yx}\mathbf{w}, (13)

whose top kk eigenvalues ρ1≥ρ2≥…≥ρk\rho_{1}\!\geq\!\rho_{2}\!\geq\!\dots\!\geq\!\rho_{k} are the canonical correlations. We report the maximum canonical correlation value (obtained from the first canonical component) as an alignment score.

PCA-assisted CCA

Since CCA method suffers from high-dimensionality data structures [45], we first project each feature vectors onto its leading rr principal components:

X~=Px⊤​X,Y~=Py⊤​Y,\displaystyle\tilde{X}=P_{x}^{\!\top}X,\qquad\tilde{Y}=P_{y}^{\!\top}Y, (14)

with Px∈ℝdx×rP_{x}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times r} (orthonormal) obtained from linear PCA or kernel PCA using an RBF kernel κ⁡(𝐳,𝐳′)=exp⁡[−γ​‖𝐳−𝐳′‖2]\kappa(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^{\prime})=\exp[-\gamma\|\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\|^{2}]. CCA is then run on X~,Y~\tilde{X},\tilde{Y}, producing more stable correlations in high-dimensional regimes. In our experiments, we used r=50r=50 (i.e., feature dimension = 50), and k=50k=50 (i.e., number of canonical components = 50).

B.2.4 SVCCA (Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis)

SVCCA [5] replaces the heuristic PCA cut-off with a data-dependent approach via SVD:

  1. 1.

    Compute SVDs: X=Ux​Σx​Vx⊤X=U_{x}\Sigma_{x}V_{x}^{\!\top}, Y=Uy​Σy​Vy⊤Y=U_{y}\Sigma_{y}V_{y}^{\!\top}.

  2. 2.

    Retain the top rx,ryr_{x},r_{y} singular vectors explaining at least a fixed proportion η\eta (e.g., 99%99\%) of variance:

    X^=Σx,[1:rx]Vx,[1:rx]⊤,Y^=Σy,[1:ry]Vy,[1:ry]⊤.\hat{X}=\Sigma_{x,[1:r_{x}]}V_{x,[1:r_{x}]}^{\!\top},\qquad\hat{Y}=\Sigma_{y,[1:r_{y}]}V_{y,[1:r_{y}]}^{\!\top}.
  3. 3.

    Run linear CCA on (X^,Y^)(\hat{X},\hat{Y}) to obtain canonical correlations {ρi}i=1k\{\rho_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} with k=min⁡(rx,ry)k=\min(r_{x},r_{y}).

The SVCCA score is reported using mean of these kk correlations, SVCCA=1k​∑i=1kρi,\text{SVCCA}=\tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\rho_{i}, where we report SVCCA score with k=10k=10.

Appendix C Spread Loss Formulation for Multimodal Framework

C.1 Our Formulation of Spread Loss for Multimodal Representation Learning

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d=12​[ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL+ℒLV]\mathcal{L}_{spread}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}\right] (15)

The formulation for VL direction is a weighted sum with α\alpha controlling the trade-off between context-level alignment and intra-context contrast:

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL=(1−α)​ℒC​o​n​C​o​n+α​ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}=(1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} (16)

For α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], per-sample case of ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}} is defined as:

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL​(ΦV,vi,B)=(1−α)​ℒC​o​n​C​o​n​(ΦV,vi,B)+α​ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E​(ΦV,vi,B)\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B)=(1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B)+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B) (17)

where

ℒC​o​n​C​o​n(ΦV,vi,B)=−1|CL​(i)|∑cl∈CL​(i)log(σ⁡(vi,cl)σ⁡(vi,cl)+∑cl~∈CL~​(i)σ⁡(vi,cl~)),\mathcal{L}_{ConCon}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B)=-\frac{1}{|C_{L}(i)|}\sum_{c_{l}\in C_{L}(i)}\log\left(\frac{\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})}{\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})+\sum_{\widetilde{c_{l}}\in\widetilde{C_{L}}(i)}\sigma(v_{i},\widetilde{c_{l}})}\right), (18)
ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E​(ΦV,vi,B)=−log⁡(σ⁡(vi,lPi)∑cl∈CL​(i)σ⁡(vi,cl)).\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B)=-\log\left(\frac{\sigma(v_{i},l_{P_{i}})}{\sum_{c_{l}\in C_{L}(i)}\sigma(v_{i},c_{l})}\right). (19)

The overall loss ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL​(ΦV,B)\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}(\Phi_{V},B) is computed by averaging over all (vi,lPi,lNi)∈B(v_{i},l_{P_{i}},l_{N_{i}})\in B:

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL​(ΦV,B)=1|B|​∑i=1|B|ℒs​p​r​e​a​d−VL​(ΦV,vi,B).\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}(\Phi_{V},B)=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i=1}^{|B|}\mathcal{L}_{spread-\text{VL}}(\Phi_{V},v_{i},B).

Recall that since hard-negative texts do not have correct corresponding images, the formulation for LV direction omits hard-negative texts. So, it follows the standard LV loss in contrastive learning scheme of CLIP models:

ℒLV(ΦL,B)=−1|B|∑i=1|B|logσ⁡(lPi,vi)∑j=1,j≠iNσ⁡(lPi,vj)\mathcal{L}_{\text{LV}}(\Phi_{L},B)=-\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i=1}^{|B|}\log\frac{\sigma(l_{P_{i}},v_{i})}{\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{N}\sigma(l_{P_{i}},v_{j})} (20)

C.2 Spread Loss Formulation in Visual Representation Learning Domain

Spread loss in vision representation learning domain [29] is constructed by a weighted sum of a supervised contrastive loss (ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\text{sup}}) [31] and a class-conditional InfoNCE loss (ℒcNCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{cNCE}}) [13]. The core motivation is similar in our multimodal scheme: training encoder to produce representations of the data by pulling together similar points (positive pairs) and pushing apart dissimilar points (negative pairs).

Formally, let BB be a batch of data from dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Define the positive set:

P⁡(i,B)={x+∈B∖{xi}:h⁡(x+)=h⁡(xi)}P(i,B)=\{x^{+}\in B\setminus\{x_{i}\}:h(x^{+})=h(x_{i})\}

and the negative set:

N⁡(i,B)={x−∈B∖{xi}:h⁡(x−)≠h⁡(xi)},N(i,B)=\{x^{-}\in B\setminus\{x_{i}\}:h(x^{-})\neq h(x_{i})\},

where h⁡(x)h(x) denotes the class label of xx and a⁡(xi)a(x_{i}) be an augmentation of xix_{i}. Define the similarity (i.e., cosine similarity) with temperature hyperparameter τ>0\tau>0:

σf​(x,x′)=exp⁡(f​(x)⊤​f​(x′)τ).\sigma_{f}(x,x^{\prime})=\exp\left(\frac{f(x)^{\top}f(x^{\prime})}{\tau}\right).

For α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], the per-sample spread loss is defined as:

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d​(f,xi,B)=(1−α)​ℒs​u​p​(f,xi,B)+α​ℒc​N​C​E​(f,xi,B),\mathcal{L}_{spread}(f,x_{i},B)=(1-\alpha)\mathcal{L}_{sup}(f,x_{i},B)+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{cNCE}(f,x_{i},B), (21)

where

ℒs​u​p(f,xi,B)=−1|P⁡(i,B)|∑x+∈P⁡(i,B)log(σf​(xi,x+)σf​(xi,x+)+∑x−∈N⁡(i,B)σf​(xi,x−)),\mathcal{L}_{sup}(f,x_{i},B)=-\frac{1}{|P(i,B)|}\sum_{x^{+}\in P(i,B)}\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{f}(x_{i},x^{+})}{\sigma_{f}(x_{i},x^{+})+\sum_{x^{-}\in N(i,B)}\sigma_{f}(x_{i},x^{-})}\right), (22)
ℒc​N​C​E​(f,xi,B)=−log⁡(σf​(xi,a⁡(xi))∑x+∈P⁡(i,B)σf​(xi,x+)).\mathcal{L}_{cNCE}(f,x_{i},B)=-\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{f}(x_{i},a(x_{i}))}{\sum_{x^{+}\in P(i,B)}\sigma_{f}(x_{i},x^{+})}\right). (23)

The overall loss ℒs​p​r​e​a​d​(f,B)\mathcal{L}_{spread}(f,B) is computed by averaging over all xi∈Bx_{i}\in B:

ℒs​p​r​e​a​d​(f,B)=1|B|​∑xi∈Bℒs​p​r​e​a​d​(f,xi,B).\mathcal{L}_{spread}(f,B)=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{x_{i}\in B}\mathcal{L}_{spread}(f,x_{i},B).

ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\text{sup}} encourages intra-class clustering by pulling together same-class samples, while ℒcNCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{cNCE}} repels within-class samples except for augmentations. Their combination spreads same-class points while preserving instance-level attraction, promoting more structured representation spaces.

C.3 Side-by-Side Comparison

Intuition.

ℒC​o​n​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{ConCon} pulls an image toward all texts that share its visual context (analogous to class-level clustering, performed by ℒs​u​p\mathcal{L}_{sup}), while ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} pushes it away from other texts inside that context except its primary caption (analogous to instance discrimination, performed by ℒc​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{cNCE}).

Table 9 summarizes the symbols used in the Spread loss in vision domain (left column) and their direct counterparts in our our multimodal formulation (right column). The first row clarifies that the visual setting relies on a single encoder f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot), whereas the multimodal variant distinguishes between an image encoder ΦV\Phi_{V} and a text encoder ΦL\Phi_{L}. Subsequent rows pair up the anchor, positive, and negative sets, making it explicit that class labels in the visual domain translate to visual contexts (collections of captions). Finally, the similarity function retains the same softmax-temperature structure; only the argument types differ (image-image vs. image–text).

Table 10 presents the four loss terms from an objective-driven perspective. Each row identifies the loss and breaks down its optimization goal into four parts: the anchor being updated, the positive samples it should align with, the negatives it should separate from, and the broader motivation behind this push-pull dynamic. This format highlights a consistent analogy: ℒs​u​p\mathcal{L}_{sup} clusters images by class, while our ℒC​o​n​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{ConCon} clusters images with all captions from the same visual context. In contrast, ℒc​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{cNCE} and ℒc​o​n​t​e​x​t​N​C​E\mathcal{L}_{contextNCE} act as sharpening losses, refining clusters by contrasting a specific positive — an augmentation for vision case and a primary caption for our multimodal case — against hard negatives.

Appendix D Model Analysis & Training Configuration

D.1 Pretrained State-of-the Art Unimodal Backbones

D.2 JAM (Joint Autoencoder Modulator) Framework

We experiment JAM (Joint Autoencoder Modulator) framework with 3 hidden layers with dimension size 512, bottleneck/latent layer with dimension size 256, drop out ratio of 0.1, batch size of 32, and SwiGLU activation. With this architecture, Table 12 shows the model analysis of JAM attached to each pretrained unimodal backbones.

With the extracted unimodal features (language and vision, respectively) data, for each task setting, we use 70-15-15 train/validation/test splits. For each task, we train our Joint Autoencoder Modulator (JAM) with all the loss schemes (ℒs​p​r​e​a​d\mathcal{L}_{spread}, ℒc​o​n\mathcal{L}_{con}, ℒN​e​g​C​o​n\mathcal{L}_{NegCon}) for 100 epochs with a batch size of 32, using data seeds 5, 42, and 55. The reported scores are the average of recall scores across different seeds. Both autoencoders are optimized jointly using AdamW [35] with gradient clipping (1.0) and a cosine annealing scheduler. We initialize the logit scaling parameter in log-space as l​o​g​(1/0.07)log(1/0.07), following the common CLIP [13] initialization strategy. During training, the effective scale is recovered via exponentiation, allowing the model to start with sharper similarity distributions and learn an appropriate temperature dynamically. The reconstruction loss is weighted by a linearly decaying factor λ⁡(t)\lambda(t), decreasing from 1.0 to 0.1 over training epochs to gradually emphasize the alignment objective. Every five epochs, we compute image-to-text Recall@1 on the validation set, applying early stopping if no improvement is observed for five consecutive validations. We evaluate on two retrieval settings: (1) binary choice between the positive and its hard negative (standard evaluation scheme in fine-grained task setting [19, 28]), and (2) a 5-way choice including three additional distractors.

Appendix E Compute Systems/Resources

All experiments were conducted in either set-ups: Apple Macbook Pro (M2 chip) or NVIDIA RTX 3080. We utilized NVIDIA RTX 3080 system for language models’ feature extraction and M2 chip system for vision models’ feature extraction. Running our JAM framework is done in both set-ups. Finetuning CLIP model is conducted in NVIDIA RTX 3080 system.
